newsitem.title: GERMANY: Kohl's revised tax reform hits more headwind.
newsitem.headline: Kohl's revised tax reform hits more headwind.

text.p: The German government's revised tax reform proposals ran into stiff headwinds on Saturday as the opposition Social Democrats and influential business lobby groups vowed to block the coalition's plans.

SPD chairman Oskar Lafontaine and parliamentary group leader Rudolf Scharping said the left-leaning party would use its veto powers in the upper house of parliament to thwart the tax reform suggestions put forward by Chancellor Helmut Kohl's coalition.

"We will not support any bill where no one knows where the financing will come," Scharping said. "This is a fraudulent tax reform. The coalition's plans are financially less sound than before. They will only tear greater holes in the budget."

Scharping told the Bild newspaper that Kohl's centre-right coalition would have to take greater steps towards the SPD's demands in order to win the party's needed support in the Bundesrat, or upper house.

The coalition was trying to win the SPD's support by amending Finance Minister Theo Waigel's plan to shake up the German tax system. But the revisions to make it more palatable appear to have satisfied no one.
Industry groups and trade unions joined the SPD in criticising the amended tax reforms agreed late on Thursday by Kohl's coalition to fill new gaps in the 1998 and 1999 budgets.
The reforms, a mixture of eliminating tax write-offs and lowering tax rates, are to be put to the Bundestag (lower house) on June 26 in a bill.

The bills, which would phase in the tax changes in 1998 and 1999, then go into the Bundesrat where they face certain defeat at the hands of the SPD. Then, from mid-July the horse-trading with the SPD will start in parliamentary mediation.
The coalition also proposes gradual tax increases on weekend and night shift work and an introduction of limits on the losses corporations could carry forward to offset future profits.

The reforms, which aim to lower tax rates for companies and individuals while making it more difficult to avoid taxes, were originally intended to reduce the overall tax burden by 30 billion marks in 1999.
"It is not going to work if new burdens on citizens are brought forward and tax relief is left behind," said Lafontaine at a rally in Dortmund.

Hans-Olaf Henkel, the president of the powerful Federation of Germany Industry (BDI), said the lobby group would oppose the coalition on the corporate loss-carryover limits. German firms now pay one of the highest marginal rates of tax in Europe.

"We supported the government's original concept on tax reform even if it did not mean tax relief for companies because we felt it sent out the right signals," Henkel told the Express newspaper on Saturday.
"But the support will disappear if this reform goes from being neutral for companies to one that we have to pay more for," Henkel said.

The Association of Wholesalers and Exporters (BGA) said on Friday the coalition's latest proposals were ill-conceived. BGA president Michael Fuchs said German businesses already paid a disproportionate share to raise state revenue and should not be asked to pay more.

Walter Riester, deputy president of Germany's largest union IG Metall, said his union was firmly opposed to phased-in taxation of night and weekend shiftwork and argued this still failed to solve Bonn's budgetary impasse.
